q-15103.name: Question 1
q-15103.problem:
Suppose that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{(-1)}^{n}}{{n}^{2}}
$$

and that ${s}_{6}$ is the sixth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-{s}_{6}|<k$ for some real number $k.$ Find the value of $k.$
q-15103.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{{(-1)}^{n}}{{n}^{2}}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is positive and decreasing for $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $6$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{6}|<|{b}_{7}|=|\frac{(-1)^{7}}{{7}^{2}}|=\frac{1}{49}.
$$

 

Therefore, $k=\frac{1}{49}.$

q-352756.problem:
Suppose that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{(-1)}^{n}\,n!}{(n+4)!}
$$

and that ${s}_{6}$ is the sixth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-{s}_{6}|<k$ for some real number $k.$ Find the value of $k.$ Do not round the answer.

$k=$

{{field-1}}
q-352756.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=\frac{n!}{(n+4)!}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{{(-1)}^{n}\,n!}{(n+4)!}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is positive and decreasing for $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $6$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{6}|<|{b}_{7}|=|\frac{{(-1)}^{7}\,7!}{(7+4)!}|=\frac{7!}{11!}=\frac{1}{8\cdot 9\cdot 10\cdot 11}=\frac{1}{7920}.
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{1}{7920}.$

q-352762.name: Question 3
q-352762.problem:
Given that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{n({n}^{2}+4)}
$$

and that ${s}_{i}$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of $i$ such that
$|S-{s}_{i}|<0.05.$

${i}^{3}+3{i}^{2}+7i+5\ge $
{{field-1}}
q-352762.worked_solution:
First, let

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{3}{n({n}^{2}+4)}\,\text{and}\,{b}_{n}=\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{n({n}^{2}+4)}.
$$

Then ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing for $n\ge 2$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ Therefore, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because the series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{i}|<|{b}_{i+1}|.
$$

Thus, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}|{b}_{i+1}|=|\frac{3(-1)^{i+2}}{(i+1)((i+1)^{2}+4)}| & \le 0.05 \\ \frac{3}{(i+1)((i+1)^{2}+4)} & \le \frac{1}{20} \\ 60 & \le (i+1)((i+1)^{2}+4) \\ 60 & \le (i+1)({i}^{2}+2i+1+4) \\ 60 & \le (i+1)({i}^{2}+2i+5) \\ 60 & \le {i}^{3}+3{i}^{2}+7i+5 \\ {i}^{3}+3{i}^{2}+7i+5 & \ge 60.\end{aligned}
$$

q-352774.name: Question 5
q-352774.problem:
Given that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=3}^{\infty }\frac{{2(-1)}^{n}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2n+1)}
$$

and that ${s}_{i}$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of $i$ such that $|S-{s}_{i}|<0.2.$

$\operatorname{ln}⁡(2i+3)\ge $
{{field-1}}
q-352774.worked_solution:
First, let ${a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2n+1)}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{{(-1)}^{n}\,2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2n+1)}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing for $n\ge 3$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test. 

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{i}|<|{b}_{i+1}|.
$$

So, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}|{b}_{i+1}|=|\frac{(-1)^{i+1}\,2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2(i+1)+1)}| & \le 0.2 \\ \frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2i+3)} & \le 0.2 \\ \frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2i+3)} & \le \frac{1}{5} \\ 10 & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(2i+3) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2i+3) & \ge 10.\end{aligned}
$$
